html:
The Bhagavad Gita, "Song of the Lord", is a 700-verse section of the Mahabharata and the best known scripture of Hinduism. Most scholars date it to the last two centuries BCE or a little later.

It is set on the battlefield of Kurukshetra just before the fighting starts. The warrior Arjuna sees his teachers and cousins in the enemy line and refuses to fight. His charioteer, Krishna, answers him, and in the course of the talk shows himself to be God.

Krishna's answer joins three paths that had been rivals:

  • action: do your duty, but give up any claim to its results;
  • knowledge: the self is not the body and cannot be killed;
  • devotion: love of God is open to everyone, whatever their birth.

The third path fed the later bhakti movement. Every major Hindu thinker, from Shankara to Ramanuja, wrote a commentary on the Gita. In the 20th century Gandhi read it daily and took from it the idea of acting without wanting the reward.
